rv.q: The stylized performances of a superb Asian-American cast — including George Takei — are ideally suited to this minimalist production of one of the great musicals of our time.
This time, Doyle — famous and/or infamous for having actors play instruments — instead keeps a small, superbly musical East-West orchestra on one end of the white ramp of a stage.
This is a lovingly mounted staging of a unique show, a sorrowful account of violation, naivety and shattered peace, and a culture clash musical imbued with solemn humanity.
The sometimes-glorious, sometimes-lackluster revival that John Doyle has staged in Classic Stage’s 200-seat Off Broadway home takes that less-is-more proposition nearly to a point of no return.
Trimmed to 90 uninterrupted minutes, it’s diminished, like listening to Beethoven through a transistor radio or looking at the moon through the wrong end of a telescope.
Striving for lean, he makes the show seem thin.
By paring the show to its roots (except, thankfully, in the music department), Doyle’s Pacific Overtures makes for altogether terrific theatergoing.
Doyle has given us a Pacific Overtures that is both delicate and tough-minded, a tensile thing of beauty that may at last find a place among Sondheim's major works.
Doyle has shaped a delicate production that's comparatively easy to parse.
Doyle has done the same with Pacific Overtures... he lovingly traces those very flaws, he observes them from every angle and he allows us to see for the first time how beautiful they are.

Nonetheless, there can be no denying that Doyle has made the story of the Westernization of Japan in the 1850s (primarily via a naval invasion led by America’s Commodore Perry) as clear as a freshly Windexed mirror.
Rarely is a musical this non-traditional and daring also executed so well, and the CSC company is an expert and engaging group of storytellers.
The sound is magnificently rich in this intimate space.
If you can navigate your way past the problems, you will find there is much to enjoy.
But this production, while scrupulously acted, seems to be having a conversation with itself, not the audience.
Doyle almost always gets it wrong, making Sondheim’s shows all about the angst.
Personally, I found the production to be a plain and unexciting affair that, for the most part, drained away rather than enhanced the musical’s impact.
If there’s such a thing as minimalist grandeur, director John Doyle achieves it with his rendering of Stephen Sondheim and John Weidman’s Pacific Overtures.
Offering a powerful lesson of the perils of change and the dangers of becoming too much like those you initially despise, “Pacific Overtures” is an eye-opening delight.
This Pacific Overtures is a shining example of “less is more.”
His bold production has the vision and clarity to do just that.
Only the greatest composer-lyricist could have conquered this task, and the greatest one indeed did.
Doyle, who’s the Classic Stage Company artistic director, has made much of his reputation thoughtfully and passionately reviving Sondheim’s musicals.
And yet this comes across as 'Pacific Overtures' light, a work that begs to be seen in its original scope.

While it would be unfair to single anyone out, this production is blessed to feature the wonderful George Takei, who brings his sonorous baritone voice and impish deadpan to the role of the Reciter, and his droll, assured presence is alone worth the price of admission.

"'Pacific Overtures' indulges in an East/West narrative that, however well-intentioned, mostly subscribes to colonialist infantilizing of the Japanese...There are very few opportunities for Asian-American actors in New York, and it is heartening to see that they make up the entire cast here...[but] I wish they had been employed on a better...
What's left is not unlike a bowl of ramen without the broth -- substance devoid of flavor.

Only ninety minutes in length, “Pacific Overtures” will I hope make you feel, as I did, that you can’t ask for more pleasure than to find yourself floating in the middle of the sea with Sondheim, Doyle and Company.
Doyle’s production tears away so many visual elements that it endangers clear comprehension of the book’s many transitions in time and place.
Too bad Doyle's unfocused production reduces a provocative piece of theater to a stale deconstruction mistaking poverty for intimacy.

cn.t: John Doyle's minimalist revival of Sondheim's complex 1976 musical divides critics: some praise the clarity and talented Asian-American cast, while others lament that heavy cuts strip away the show's epic grandeur and emotional heart.
